column3: PRS-CS score from the 2014 PGC schizophrenia GWAS; in four US health systems each standard deviation raised the odds of a diagnosis about 1.5 times (top tenth up to 4.6 times the bottom tenth), yet most people with a high score never develop it.

SDPR score from the 2018 PGC bipolar GWAS (about 20,000 cases); it has not been tested against bipolar diagnoses in the catalog, scores like it explain only a few percent of liability, and most people with a high score never develop it.

PRS-CS score from the 2019 depression GWAS of about 807,000 people; in a US hospital biobank it explained about 2 percent of the variation in who had a depression diagnosis, so it nudges risk rather than predicting it.
LDpred2 score trained on UK Biobank anxiety-disorder diagnoses (ICD-10 F41); each standard deviation raised the odds of a diagnosis only about 1.2 times, so it is a weak signal.

Score built from the 2019 PGC ADHD GWAS (about 20,000 cases) by clumping and a p-value cutoff; in European-ancestry children it was only weakly linked to ADHD symptoms, so it says little about any one person.

Score from the 2019 iPSYCH-PGC autism GWAS; each standard deviation raised the odds of autism about 1.3 times and it explained about 2.5 percent of the variation, so most people with a high score are not autistic.
LDpred2 score trained on about 390,000 UK Biobank Europeans; it explains about 4 percent of the variation in the neuroticism questionnaire (a tendency toward worry, moodiness and negative feelings).
LDpred2 score from the UK Biobank general happiness question, oriented so a higher score means rating oneself less happy; it explains only about 1 percent of the variation.

PRS-CS score from a meta-analysis of UK Biobank and Million Veteran Program insomnia GWAS (about 870,000 Europeans); each standard deviation raised the odds of insomnia symptoms about 1.3 times in independent US cohorts.
LDpred2 score from the UK Biobank morning or evening person question, oriented so a higher score means more of a night owl; it explains about 5 percent of the variation.
LDpred2 score trained on years of schooling in UK Biobank; it explains about 4 percent of the variation, and part of that reflects family and social environment rather than the person's own biology.

LDpred2-auto score trained on the UK Biobank fluid intelligence test (verbal and numerical reasoning); it explains about 5 percent of the variation in test scores, so it says little about any one person's ability.
LDpred2 score trained on UK Biobank household income; it explains about 3 percent of the variation and largely overlaps the education score rather than anything specific to money.

PRS-CS score from the 2019 Karlsson Linner GWAS of a combined risky-behaviour measure (speeding, drinking, smoking and number of sexual partners), not self-rated risk tolerance; it explained under 2 percent of the variation in alcohol-problem symptoms in an independent sample.
LDpred2 score trained on UK Biobank, oriented so a higher score means a later age at first sexual intercourse; it explains about 6 percent of the variation.
LDpred score from the 2022 GSCAN GWAS of about 670,000 Europeans; it explained about 1 percent of the variation in weekly drinking in an independent US sample, so habits and setting matter far more.

LDpred score from the 2022 GSCAN GWAS of ever smoking regularly (about 805,000 Europeans); in one independent US sample it explained up to about 10 percent of the variation, but whether someone starts depends heavily on circumstances.
LDpred2 score trained on the UK Biobank ever-taken-cannabis question; it explains under 1 percent of the variation, so it is a very weak signal.

PRS-CS score from a small GWAS of healthy thin people (STILTS study); each standard deviation raised the odds of being thin only about 1.2 times in UK Biobank, and it largely mirrors the BMI score in reverse.
LDpred2-auto score trained on about 160,000 UK Biobank men; it explains about 9 percent of the variation in male blood testosterone and is not meaningful for women.
